1. Meaning of Centre–State Relations

Centre–State Relations refer to the constitutional relationship between:

  • Union Government.
  • State Governments.

The Constitution regulates their:

  • Legislative interaction.
  • Administrative interaction.
  • Financial interaction.
  • Inter-governmental coordination.

The objective is to maintain a balance between:

  • National unity.
  • State autonomy.

2. Constitutional Basis

Important constitutional provisions include:

  • Articles 245–255 → Legislative relations.
  • Articles 256–263 → Administrative relations.
  • Articles 268–293 → Financial relations.
  • Articles 301–307 → Inter-State trade and commerce.
  • Articles 352, 356 and 360 → Emergency provisions.
  • Seventh Schedule → Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
📌 Must-Memorise

Legislative → 245–255

Administrative → 256–263

Financial → 268–293

3. Nature of the Relationship

Centre–State Relations combine:

  • Federal division of powers.
  • Administrative coordination.
  • Financial interdependence.
  • Constitutional supervision.
  • Cooperative governance.

4. Constitutional Status of States

  • States are not administrative departments of the Union.

Each State possesses its own:

  • Executive.
  • Legislature.
  • Administrative machinery.
  • Financial responsibilities.

However, State authority remains subject to:

  • Constitution.
  • Constitutional powers of Parliament.
  • Judicial review.

5. Strong Union Features

Important strong-Union features include:

  • Residuary powers with Parliament.
  • Parliamentary power over State List in exceptional situations.
  • Union directions to States.
  • Governors appointed by President.
  • All India Services.
  • Emergency provisions.
  • Greater access of Union to major financial resources.

6. Protection of State Autonomy

State autonomy is protected through:

  • State List.
  • Elected State Legislatures.
  • State Council of Ministers.
  • Independent constitutional powers.
  • Rajya Sabha representation.
  • State ratification of specified constitutional amendments.
  • Judicial review of unconstitutional Union action.

7. Practical Interdependence

Union and States frequently cooperate in areas such as:

  • Public health.
  • Education.
  • Agriculture.
  • Disaster management.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Environmental protection.
  • Economic development.
  • Internal security.

8. Constitutional Supremacy

  • Both Union and States derive authority from the Constitution.
  • Neither Parliament nor State Legislature may exceed its constitutional competence.
  • Constitutional disputes may be examined by the Judiciary.

9. Supreme Court and Federal Disputes

The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction in specified disputes involving:

  • Union and one or more States.
  • Two or more States.

This helps preserve:

  • Constitutional distribution of powers.
  • Federal balance.

10. Article 245

Article 245 provides:

  • Parliament may make laws for whole or any part of India.
  • State Legislature may make laws for whole or any part of that State.

13. Union List

Parliament normally has exclusive power over subjects of national importance such as:

  • Defence.
  • Foreign Affairs.
  • Currency.
  • Banking.
  • Railways.
  • Citizenship.
  • Atomic Energy.
  • Telecommunications.

14. State List

State Legislatures normally possess legislative authority over matters such as:

  • Public Order.
  • Police.
  • Agriculture.
  • Public Health.
  • Local Government.
  • Land.
  • Irrigation.
  • Markets and Fairs.

15. Concurrent List

Both Parliament and State Legislatures may legislate on matters such as:

  • Criminal Law.
  • Criminal Procedure.
  • Marriage and Divorce.
  • Education.
  • Forests.
  • Labour Welfare.
  • Electricity.
  • Economic and Social Planning.

16. Priority among Legislative Lists

The constitutional scheme gives priority to:

  • Union List over competing State or Concurrent fields where constitutionally applicable.
  • Concurrent List over State List where overlap arises within the constitutional framework.

31. General Rule of Repugnancy

If both valid laws conflict:

  • Parliamentary law normally prevails.
  • State law becomes inoperative to the extent of inconsistency.

32. Presidential Assent Exception

If a State law on a Concurrent List matter:

  • Is reserved for President.
  • Receives Presidential assent.

it may prevail:

  • Within that State.

33. Parliament's Later Power

Even after Presidential assent to the State law:

  • Parliament may subsequently enact another law overriding it.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

State Law + Presidential Assent → May Prevail in State

Parliament → Can Later Override

34. Doctrine of Repugnancy

Repugnancy may arise where:

  • Union and State laws occupy same legislative field.
  • Compliance with one leads to violation of the other.
  • Parliament intends to occupy the entire field.

35. Doctrine of Territorial Nexus

A State law may affect persons or transactions outside the State where there is:

  • Sufficient.
  • Real.
  • Substantial connection
  • between the State and the subject matter.
📌 Must-Memorise

Territorial Nexus → Real Connection between State and Subject Matter

36. Doctrine of Colourable Legislation

This doctrine means:

  • Legislature cannot indirectly do what it cannot constitutionally do directly.

The principle is expressed as:

  • What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.

37. Doctrine of Pith and Substance

When a law touches more than one legislative field:

Courts examine its:

  • True nature.
  • Dominant purpose.
  • Incidental encroachment does not automatically invalidate the law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pith and Substance → True Nature of Legislation

Where entries appear to overlap:

  • Courts attempt to interpret them harmoniously.
  • The objective is to preserve both legislative fields as far as possible.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

What are Centre–State Relations? → Constitutional legislative, administrative and financial relations between Union and State Governments.

Which Articles deal with Legislative Relations? → Articles 245–255.

Which Articles principally deal with Administrative Relations? → Articles 256–263.

Which Articles principally deal with Financial Relations? → Articles 268–293.

Which Schedule distributes legislative subjects? → Seventh Schedule.

What are its three Lists? → Union List, State List and Concurrent List.

Are States merely administrative departments of Union? → No.

Which Article deals with territorial extent of legislative powers? → Article 245.

Can Parliament legislate for whole India? → Yes.

Can State Legislature normally legislate for another State? → No.

Which doctrine permits some extra-State effect where sufficient connection exists? → Territorial Nexus.

Which Article distributes legislative powers among the three Lists? → Article 246.

Who possesses residuary powers? → Parliament.

Which Article? → Article 248.

Which Union List Entry is associated with residuary power? → Entry 97.

Which Article allows Parliament to legislate on State List in national interest? → Article 249.

Which House must pass the resolution? → Rajya Sabha.

What majority is required? → Not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.

How long does an Article 249 resolution remain in force? → One year.

Can it be renewed? → Yes.

How long does the resulting Parliamentary law continue after the resolution ceases? → Six months.

Which Article allows Parliament to legislate on State List during National Emergency? → Article 250.

How long does such a law ordinarily continue after Emergency ends? → Six months.

Which Article permits Parliament to legislate at request of two or more States? → Article 252.

Can another State later adopt such law? → Yes.

Can a participating State Legislature unilaterally amend an Article 252 Parliamentary law? → No.

Which Article permits legislation to implement international treaties? → Article 253.

Can Parliament legislate on State List under Article 253? → Yes.

Which Article governs repugnancy? → Article 254.

What is the general rule? → Parliamentary law prevails.

What happens if State law receives Presidential assent? → It may prevail within that State.

Can Parliament later override it? → Yes.

What is Doctrine of Colourable Legislation? → Legislature cannot indirectly do what it cannot directly do.

What is Doctrine of Pith and Substance? → Court examines true nature and dominant purpose of legislation.

What is Territorial Nexus? → Sufficient real connection between State and subject matter.

Which Article requires States to comply with Parliamentary laws? → Article 256.

Which Article prevents State executive power from impeding Union executive power? → Article 257.

Which Article allows Union functions to be entrusted to States? → Article 258.

Who acts under Article 258? → President with State consent.

Which Article permits State functions to be entrusted to Union? → Article 258A.

Who acts under Article 258A? → Governor with Union consent.

Which Article creates constitutional basis for Inter-State Council? → Article 263.

When was Inter-State Council established? → 1990.

On whose recommendation? → Sarkaria Commission.

Who chairs it? → Prime Minister.

Are Zonal Councils constitutional bodies? → No.

What are they? → Statutory bodies.

Under which Act? → States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

Who chairs Zonal Councils? → Union Home Minister.

Which Article permits creation of All India Services? → Article 312.

What majority does Rajya Sabha require? → Not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.

Name the three All India Services in the attachment. → IAS, IPS and IFoS.

Which Article imposes duty on Union to protect States? → Article 355.

Protect against what? → External aggression and internal disturbance.

What additional duty exists under Article 355? → Ensure State Government is carried on according to Constitution.

Which Article deals with duties levied by Union but collected and appropriated by States? → Article 268.

Which Article deals with taxes levied and collected by Union and assigned to States? → Article 269.

Which Article deals with GST on inter-State supplies? → Article 269A.

Which Amendment inserted Article 269A? → 101st Amendment, 2016.

Which Article deals with distribution of Central taxes? → Article 270.

What is this sharing called? → Tax Devolution.

Which institution recommends tax devolution? → Finance Commission.

Which Article permits Union surcharge? → Article 271.

Who receives surcharge proceeds? → Union Government.

Which Article deals with Grants-in-Aid? → Article 275.

Which Article establishes GST Council? → Article 279A.

Who chairs GST Council? → Union Finance Minister.

Which Article establishes Finance Commission? → Article 280.

Who constitutes Finance Commission? → President.

How often? → Every five years or earlier if necessary.

What is Finance Commission's composition stated in the attachment? → One Chairperson and four other members.

What does Finance Commission recommend? → Tax devolution, Grants-in-Aid and measures to augment State funds for Local Bodies.

Which Article deals with Union borrowing? → Article 292.

Which Article deals with State borrowing? → Article 293.

When may State borrowing require Central Government consent according to the attachment? → When the State is indebted to the Union under the constitutional framework.

When was NITI Aayog established? → 2015.

What did it replace? → Planning Commission.

What forms of federalism does NITI Aayog promote? → Cooperative and Competitive Federalism.

Which Amendment reorganised States? → 7th Amendment, 1956.

Which Commission preceded it? → States Reorganisation Commission or Fazl Ali Commission.

Which Amendment transferred five subjects from State List to Concurrent List? → 42nd Amendment, 1976.

Which five subjects are identified in the attachment? → Education, Forests, Protection of Wild Animals and Birds, Weights and Measures, and Administration of Justice/organisation of courts except Supreme Court and High Courts.

Which Amendment restored Emergency safeguards? → 44th Amendment, 1978.

Which Amendment strengthened tax devolution? → 80th Amendment, 2000.

Which Amendment historically inserted Article 268A for Service Tax? → 88th Amendment, 2003.

Which Amendment introduced GST? → 101st Amendment, 2016.

Which Articles did it insert according to the attachment? → Articles 246A, 269A and 279A.

Which Amendment gave constitutional status to NCBC? → 102nd Amendment, 2018.

Which Amendment restored States' power to identify SEBCs? → 105th Amendment, 2021.

Which case explained the nature of the Indian Union? → State of West Bengal v. Union of India, 1963.

Which case clarified residuary powers? → Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon, 1972.

Which case established Basic Structure Doctrine? → Kesavananda Bharati, 1973.

Is Federalism part of Basic Structure according to the attachment? → Yes.

Which 1977 case dealt with constitutional limits on Union action toward State Governments? → State of Rajasthan v. Union of India.

Which is the most important Centre–State case in the attachment? → S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, 1994.

Which Article was central in S.R. Bommai? → Article 356.

What major principles did Bommai establish? → Federalism is Basic Structure, Article 356 is judicially reviewable and majority should ordinarily be tested on Assembly floor.

Which case held domicile in concerned State is unnecessary for Rajya Sabha election? → Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India, 2006.

Which 2018 case emphasised Cooperative Federalism and constitutional morality in Delhi? → State (NCT of Delhi) v. Union of India.

Which 2023 case dealt with executive control over services in Delhi? → Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India.

What is the simplest way to remember Centre–State Relations? → Legislative powers are constitutionally divided, administrative powers are coordinated, and financial resources are constitutionally shared.
